The sages sat in quiet meditation, their presence unmoving like the river beside them. The flow of the Gaṅgā (गङ्गा), steady and unceasing, seemed to whisper the story of time itself. Before them, King Parīkṣit (परिक्षित्), no longer burdened by the weight of kingship, listened in deep contemplation. In the stillness of that sacred moment, he reflected on the vast questions that stirred his heart—the nature of the universe, the movement of time, and the place of mortal beings within it.

He had heard of realms beyond the physical world, of planes that existed in layers unseen to the eye, of ages that passed like fleeting moments in the eyes of the creator. Now, he yearned to understand how this universe came into being, how time flowed across its expanse, and how human life found its place in the midst of such immensity.

Śuka Mahārṣi (शुकमहर्षिः), seated among the sages, understood the unspoken questions stirring in the king's heart. He began to explain that to comprehend the eternal, one must first grasp the framework upon which the universe is structured. The ancient sages, far from being mere mystics, had mapped the cosmos with extraordinary precision. Their understanding of time and space was not abstract but deeply measured—reflected in every rite, every prayer, every calculation of the stars. Even the most basic of rituals began with the Saṅkalpa (सङ्कल्प)—a formal declaration of intention that located the performer not only on Earth but within the vast tapestry of cosmic time.

The Saṅkalpa, he noted, was more than a ritual formula. It situated the speaker within the great wheel of creation, giving voice to one’s temporal and spatial coordinates. A traditional recitation might go:
Adya Brahmaṇaḥ dvitīya-parārddhe Śveta-varāha-kalpe Vaivasvata-manvantare aṣṭāviṁśatitame Kali-yuge prathama-pāde Jambu-dvīpe Bhārata-varṣe Bhārata-khaṇḍe…

This, translated, marked the precise moment of the act: in the second half of Brahmā’s (ब्रह्मा) lifespan, during the Śveta Varāha Kalpa (श्वेतवराहकल्प), within the Vaivasvata Manvantara (वैवस्वतमन्वन्तर), in the 28th cycle of the Kali Yuga (कलियुग), in its first quarter, upon Jambu-dvīpa (जम्बूद्वीप), within the land of Bhārata-varṣa (भारतवर्ष). Such a declaration was not poetic excess but reflected a precise cosmology—an exact understanding of where and when one stood in the vast ocean of space-time.

This attention to time was part of a broader cosmic vision. According to the ancient sages, all of existence was arranged in sacred order, structured around the Śiśumāra Cakram (शिशुमार चक्रम्), the celestial form of the Supreme—shaped like a great dolphin or whale encircling the stars. This cosmic being held the planets and realms within its body. At its heart lay Dhruvaloka (ध्रुवलोक), the unshakable realm of Dhruva Mahārāja (ध्रुवमहाराज), the pole star. Around it revolved the planets, including the domains of Indra (इन्द्र), Agni (अग्नि), and Dharma (धर्म), as well as the seven sages—the Saptarṣis (सप्तर्षि)—whose presence governed the rhythm of cosmic time. The constellations, seen by mortals as star-patterns for agriculture or navigation, were understood by the seers as markers in a divine body, each with purpose and place.

Beyond the Śiśumāra lay the great Brahmāṇḍa (ब्रह्माण्ड), the cosmic egg that contained all of manifest existence. Within it unfolded multiple realms: Bhūloka (भूलोक), the realm of mortals; Bhuvarloka (भुवर्लोक), the intermediary sphere of spirits and celestial travel; Svargaloka (स्वर्गलोक), the heavenly realm of the Devas (देवाः); and, rising above, Maharloka (महरलोक), Janaloka (जनलोक), Tapoloka (तपोलोक), and Satyaloka (सत्यलोक), the highest, where Brahmā himself presides over creation.

Below Bhūloka extended the nether realms—Atala (अतल), Vitala (वितल), Sutala (सुतल), Rasātala (रसातल), Talātala (तलातल), Mahātala (महातल), and Pātāla (पाताल)—each a domain of beings and powers mostly hidden from mortal experience, yet essential to the fabric of the cosmos.

If the structure of the universe was vast, so too was the conception of time. In human life, time was fleeting—a matter of days, years, or decades. But in the divine realms, it flowed differently. One day in Svargaloka equated to an entire year on Earth. A single day of Brahmā spanned a thousand cycles of the four Yugas: Satya (सत्य), Tretā (त्रेता), Dvāpāra (द्वापर), and Kali (कलि). His night was equally long. Even Brahmā, for all his creative power, was not beyond time. When his hundred celestial years concluded, even he would dissolve, and the universe would collapse into dormancy before the cycle began anew.

To Parīkṣit, this perspective was at once humbling and illuminating. What, then, was the role of a single life, a single king, a single battle? What purpose did it serve in the grand churn of cosmic time? But the vision did not end in despair or insignificance. Rather, it pointed beyond the temporal to the eternal.

All things, no matter how mighty, were bound to time—empires, sages, even the gods. But beyond time, beyond space, beyond even the Śiśumāra Cakram, there existed One who was not subject to these movements. Resting upon the ocean of eternity, this Supreme Being was untouched by change, sustaining all with silent stillness.

In the presence of the sages, by the side of the Gaṅgā, Parīkṣit was not merely a king awaiting death. He was a seeker being led toward the highest truth.




Scientific Accuracy and Significance

The ancient Vedic understanding of time and space, as embedded in the Saṅkalpa and cosmological frameworks, demonstrates a level of insight that aligns in remarkable ways with modern scientific discovery.

Yugas and Relativity: The differing time scales across realms reflect concepts akin to Einstein’s theory of relativity. Just as a day for the Devas equals a year on Earth, modern physics acknowledges that time moves differently depending on speed and gravitational influence.

Śiśumāra and Galactic Motion: The Śiśumāra Cakram, with Dhruvaloka at its center, echoes the galactic model with a fixed pole star and revolving bodies—a concept long used in navigation and astronomy.

Brahmāṇḍa and the Expanding Universe: The Brahmāṇḍa parallels the Big Bang model, suggesting a universe that originates, expands, and eventually contracts. The idea of repeating cosmic cycles also resonates with current theories in quantum cosmology.

Precision in the Saṅkalpa: By positioning an individual within Kalpa, Manvantara, and Yuga, the Saṅkalpa demonstrates an advanced calendrical and astronomical system. This ability to contextualize ritual action within universal time shows both philosophical depth and observational accuracy.

In this convergence of narration and cosmology, the ancient sages emerge not only as seers but as scientists of spirit and matter—explorers of the seen and unseen alike. Their legacy offers both a map of the stars and a mirror for the soul.
